title: CRLF hell: the diff that shows every line changed
summary: Someone opened a file in a Windows editor and now git says all 200 lines changed. Understand what git stores, what it checks out, and fix it with .gitattributes instead of per-machine settings.
mental_model: Git stores line endings exactly as you commit them. `text=auto` says: normalise to LF inside the repository, and convert on checkout to whatever the platform wants. Without it, the repo ends up with a mix and every cross-platform diff is noise.

commit.message: Add config and script with LF endings

steps.title: Check what is stored versus what is on disk
steps.why: `ls-files --eol` prints two things per file: `i/` is the index (what git stored) and `w/` is the working tree (what is on your disk). Right now both say lf. This command is the whole diagnostic.

steps.title: Simulate the Windows editor
steps.why: A colleague opens config.ini in an editor that saves CRLF. Not one character of content changed, but every single line now differs at the byte level — and git compares bytes.
steps.expect: config.ini modified, w/crlf against i/lf, and the diff claims all four lines changed.

steps.title: See the noise a reviewer would see
steps.why: `--ignore-cr-at-eol` proves there is no real change. A pull request full of these is unreviewable, which is why teams that skip .gitattributes eventually lose a day to it.
steps.expect: Zero changes when carriage returns are ignored, four when they are not.

steps.title: Fix it at the repository level, not the machine level
steps.why: `core.autocrlf` is a per-machine setting, so it only works if every person configures it identically — they never do. `.gitattributes` ships with the repo and binds everyone, including CI.

write.content:
# Normalise everything to LF in the repository.
* text=auto

# Shell scripts must stay LF even on Windows checkouts.
*.sh text eol=lf

# Windows-only files stay CRLF.
*.bat text eol=crlf

# Never touch binaries.
*.png binary

commands: git commit -m "Normalise line endings via gitattributes"

steps.title: Renormalise the files already in history
steps.why: New rules do not retroactively change what is stored. `git add --renormalize .` re-reads every file through the new attributes and stages the corrected version — a one-time cleanup commit every project needs exactly once.
steps.expect: i/lf again for config.ini — git stores LF regardless of what your editor writes.

verify.label: config.ini is stored with LF in the index
verify.hint: add .gitattributes with `* text=auto`, then git add --renormalize .

steps.title: Prove the noise is gone
steps.why: Rewriting the file with CRLF again now produces no diff at all: git normalises on the way in. The editor can do whatever it likes and history stays clean.
steps.expect: Nothing. The CRLF file matches the LF blob after normalisation.

verify.label: .gitattributes is committed, so the rule travels with the repo
the catch-all normalisation rule is present
no phantom modifications remain
verify.hint: after renormalising, a CRLF file on disk should produce no diff

pitfalls: `core.autocrlf=true` fixes it on your machine and nowhere else. Ship `.gitattributes` instead.
A `.sh` file checked out with CRLF fails in Linux containers with a baffling `\r: not found`. Pin it with `eol=lf`.
Marking a file `binary` disables both diffing and line-ending conversion — right for images, wrong for text you want to review.
The renormalisation commit touches nearly every file. Land it on its own, never mixed with real changes.
cheatsheet: index and working-tree line endings, per file
normalise to LF in the repo, convert on checkout
force LF on checkout regardless of platform
restage everything through the current attributes
prove a diff is only line endings
